source_text: Ipsam animam ipsumque corpus in saeculo isto èXPOsitum omnibus ad iniuriam gerimus eiusque iniuriae patientiam summus: minorum delibatione laedemur? absit \'a seruo Christi tale inquinamentum, ut patientia maioribus temptationinus praeparata in friuolis excidat! si manu quis temptauerit prouocare, praesto est dominica monela: uerberanti te, inquit, in faciem etiam alteram genam obuerte. fatigetur improbitas patientia tua; quiuis ictus illi sit dolore et contumelia constrictus. plus improbum illum caedis sustinendo, grauius a domino uapulaturum; ab eo enim uapulabit, cuius gratia sustines. si linguae amaritudo maledicto siue conuicio eruperit, respice dictum: cum uos maledixerint, gaudete. dominus ipse maledictus in lege est et tamen solus est benedictus. igitur dominum serui consequamur et maledicamur patienter, ut benedicti esse possimus. si parum aequanimiter audiam dictum aliquod in me proteruum aut nequam, reddam et ipse amaritudinis uicem necesse est, aut cruciabor impatientia muta. cum ergo (re)percussero maledictis, quomodo secutus inueniar doctrinam domini, qua traditum est non uasculorum inquinamentis, sed eorum, quae ex ore promuntur, hominem communicari, item: manere nos omnis uani et superuacui dicti reatum? sequitur ergo, ut a quo nos dominus arcet, idem ab alio aequanimiter pati admoneat. hic iam uide patientiae uoluptatem. nam omnis iniuria, seu lingua seu manu incussa, cum patientiam offenderit, eodem exitu dispungetur, quo telum aliquod in petra constantissimae duritiae libratum et obtusum. concidet enim ibidem inrita opera et infructuosa et nonnumquam repercussum in eum, qui misit, reciproco impetu saeuiet. nempe idcirco quis te, laedit, ut doleas, quia fructus laedentis in dolore laesi est. ergo cum fructum eius euerteris non dolendo, ipse doleat necesse est amissione fructus sui. tunc tu non modo inlaesus abis, quod etiam solum tibi sufficit, sed insuper aduersarii tui et frustratione oblectatus et dolore defensus. haec est patientiae utilitas et uoluptas.
thought_title: Bearing wrongs patiently as the Lord taught
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Christians on how to endure wrongs and insults, after contrasting Christian and pagan attitudes toward loss.
pass_a_gloss: We carry the very soul and the very body in this world exposed to all for wrong, and we take up patience of that wrong as the highest thing. Will we be harmed by the tasting of lesser things? Far be it from a servant of Christ such a defilement, that patience prepared for greater temptations should fail in trifles! If anyone with the hand tries to provoke, the Lord's admonition is at hand: to the one striking you, he says, on the face, turn also the other cheek. Let shamelessness be wearied by your patience. Whatever blow it may be, let it be constrained by pain and insult. You strike that shameless man more by enduring, he will be beaten more heavily by the Lord; for he will be beaten by him, by whose grace you endure. If the bitterness of the tongue has burst out in a curse or in abuse, look back at the saying: when they curse you, rejoice. The Lord himself is cursed in the law and yet he alone is blessed. Therefore let us servants follow the Lord and let us be cursed patiently, so that we may be able to be blessed. If I hear with too little calmness some shameless or worthless word against me, I must either return in turn the bitterness, or I will be tortured by silent impatience. Therefore when I strike back with curses, how will I be found to have followed the teaching of the Lord, by which it has been handed down that a man is defiled not by the unclean things of vessels, but by those things which are brought forth from the mouth, and likewise that we remain in the guilt of every vain and superfluous word? Therefore it follows that from what the Lord keeps us away, the same he admonishes us to suffer calmly from another. Here now see the pleasure of patience. For every wrong, whether inflicted by tongue or by hand, when it has struck against patience, will be settled with the same outcome as some weapon aimed at a rock of most constant hardness and blunted. For it will fall there, a work without effect and fruitless, and sometimes struck back against him who sent it, it will rage with a returning force. Surely for this reason someone hurts you, so that you may grieve, because the fruit of the one hurting is in the grief of the one hurt. Therefore when you overturn his fruit by not grieving, he himself must grieve at the loss of his fruit. Then you not only go away unharmed, which even alone is enough for you, but in addition you are delighted by the frustration of your adversary and defended by his grief. This is the usefulness and pleasure of patience.

choices.english: we take up patience of that wrong as the highest thing
choices.why: Keeps the literal force of 'summus' as predicate adjective with 'patientiam' as object of an implied verb of taking up or practicing; preserves the superlative sense.
The rare noun 'delibatio' means a tasting or sampling; 'tasting of lesser things' keeps the metaphor of small preliminary losses.

choices.english: let shamelessness be wearied by your patience
choices.why: Preserves the passive jussive subjunctive 'fatigetur' and the instrumental ablative 'patientia tua'.
rejected: your patience should wear out shamelessness
wear down shamelessness with your patience

choices.why: 'Dispungo' is a bookkeeping term for settling or discharging an account; 'settled' keeps the financial metaphor of the wrong being discharged with the same outcome as a blunted weapon.
Keeps the literal 'go away' of 'abis' and the adjective 'unharmed'.

choices.english: delighted by the frustration of your adversary and defended by his grief
choices.why: Preserves the two passive participles with their ablatives of cause, keeping the parallel structure.
rejected: pleased by his frustration and protected by his pain
enjoying his frustration and defended by his grief

pass_b_english: We carry our very soul and body through this world exposed to every kind of wrong, and we take up patience of that wrong as the highest thing. Shall we be wounded by the tasting of lesser things? Far be it from a servant of Christ to have such a stain, that patience prepared for greater temptations should fail in trifles! If someone tries to provoke you with his hand, the Lord's admonition is ready: "If anyone strikes you on the face," he says, "turn the other cheek also" (Matthew 5:39). Let shamelessness be wearied by your patience; whatever blow he lands, let him be bound fast by pain and disgrace. You strike that shameless man more by enduring, and he will be beaten more severely by the Lord; for he will be beaten by the one for whose sake you endure. If the bitterness of a tongue bursts out in cursing or insult, look to the saying: "When they curse you, rejoice" (Matthew 5:11). The Lord himself was cursed in the law, and yet he alone is blessed. Therefore let us servants follow the Lord and be cursed patiently, so that we may be able to be blessed. If I hear some shameless or wicked word spoken against me with too little calm, I must either return bitterness in kind, or be tormented by silent impatience. So when I strike back with curses, how will I be found to have followed the Lord's teaching, by which it was handed down that a person is defiled not by the uncleanness of vessels but by the things that come out of the mouth (Matthew 15:11), and likewise that we remain guilty of every empty and idle word (Matthew 12:36)? It follows, then, that the very thing from which the Lord restrains us, he also warns us to endure calmly from another. Now see the pleasure of patience. For every wrong, whether inflicted by tongue or by hand, when it strikes against patience, will be settled with the same outcome as a weapon aimed at a rock of the firmest hardness and blunted. It will fall there, its work void and fruitless, and sometimes it will be driven back and rage with returning force against the one who sent it. Surely the reason someone harms you is so that you will grieve, because the fruit of the one who harms lies in the grief of the one harmed. Therefore when you overturn his fruit by not grieving, he himself must grieve at the loss of his fruit. Then you not only go away unharmed—which alone would be enough for you—but beyond that, you are delighted by the frustration of your adversary and defended by his grief. This is the usefulness and the pleasure of patience.
notes: The source has 'èXPOsitum' with mixed case and a grave accent on the e, likely OCR damage for 'expositum'.
The source has 'temptationinus' which appears to be an OCR error for 'temptationibus' (temptations).
The source has '(re)percussero' with parentheses around 're', indicating editorial restoration of the prefix.
